content: The test image shows two corn stalks with prominent dark black/blue-black discoloration on the outer rind of the stalk, with tan/yellow patches. This is clearly a stalk rot disease. The shiny black external discoloration is highly characteristic of Anthracnose stalk rot. Let me compare reference images.

The Anthracnose stalk rot reference shows tan/brown external and shredded internal. Charcoal stalk rot shows gray internal shredding. The test image has jet-black external rind discoloration — let me check Physoderma stalk rot and Diplodia.
Physoderma stalk rot (lower-left) shows very dark blackened stalk base — close match. Let me also check Bacterial stalk rot and the Anthracnose leaf spot/top dieback.

**Visual Analysis Summary:**
- **Affected part**: Stalk (two stalks laid out, leaf sheaths partially removed)
- **Key features**: Extensive jet-black/blue-black shiny discoloration on the outer rind of the stalk, with yellowish-tan patches where healthy tissue remains
- **Pattern**: Dark coloration covers most of the stalk surface along the internodes

**Differential Assessment:**
- **Anthracnose stalk rot**: Classic hallmark is shiny black external rind discoloration — matches very well
- **Charcoal stalk rot**: Internal gray shredded pith, not external black rind — doesn't match
- **Physoderma stalk rot**: Dark blackening concentrated at crown/nodes — partial match but less extensive
- **Diplodia stalk rot**: Tan/brown discoloration, not jet-black — doesn't match
- **Bacterial stalk rot**: Water-soaked lesions, plant collapse — doesn't match

The jet-black, shiny discoloration of the entire external rind along the stalk is the pathognomonic sign of Anthracnose stalk rot (*Colletotrichum graminicola*). The Anthracnose stalk rot reference (upper-right quadrant) shows this same internal darkening pattern after stalk is cut, consistent with the disease progression shown.
